Welcome everyone. (Introduce yourself briefly)
First I want to thank Elisabeth to let me talk about my hobbies here with you cause,
This talk is about how you can build amazing software with AI.
3:
If you're thinking about building something private with AI, here are some good reasons. I've spent the last 6 months on projects like this.

The first reason is personal: take back the joy of developing. As AI releases get better and better, that feeling can get lost. A hobby project lets you build applications you could never have built before.

Other questions I wanted to answer.
• Can a real app or game be built with AI first?
• Will a larger project get more and more bugs: does it stay scalable and stable, or get sloppy over time?
• How much supervision does it need?
• And: how can you become a better prompt programmer?

My examples: a chess engine, then a jetpack multiplayer 2D platform retro game, then a 3D first-person, six-degrees-of-freedom sci-fi game, inspired by Descent, which I played a lot in the 90s.
4: Spoiler first: these are some of the the lessons you can take with you. The rest of the talk shows where they come from.
5:
I started coding as a kid in the 80s.

Before going professional in 2001, I spent a few years as a math and chemistry teacher.

After I studied again, (system development) I got hired at OMX and later product companies, med tech and consulting. I came to SEB two and a half years ago and have been a developer in the HULT team since.

Programming has always been my hobby too. I've spent far too many hours improving my chess engines over the years.

I have two grown daughters, and I got married this spring.
6:
My advice for a hobby project: pick a goal you can measure. Mine was to get ranked on CCRL, the site that rates computer chess engines, at 2000 Elo.

Quick note on Elo: it's a rating where the gap between two players predicts the result. 200 points stronger means you score roughly 75%. A beginner is around 800, a strong club player around 2000, and grandmasters start at about 2500.

My first engine was in VB.net and never made a good move. I read up on the theory and the pseudocode and kept going. Second attempt, in C#: better moves, but too slow. Third attempt in plain C was about 40 times faster. That's ChessMatrix: Elo 1863, around place 700 on CCRL. Close, but not quite there.

This summer I built ZeroG with Antigravity and Gemini 3.6 Flash. If you try this, break the work into small steps, the same ones you'd take if you wrote it yourself. Unit test, performance test and refactor everything. And gate every change: no commit without 400 games against the previous version, with a significant improvement.

Result: Elo 2666, place 398 on CCRL. Over 800 Elo stronger than years of my own work. That shows how incredibly helpful AI can be.

What you can expect: with good unit tests the AI rarely gets things wrong. As the engine gets stronger, the problem changes. The AI's changes simply stop improving strength. The gate rejects them, not because they're buggy, but because they don't make it play better.

Also expect it to handle hard bugs. At one point the engine started playing invalid moves. That kind of bug used to be a nightmare for me, because the search functions are long, complicated and recursive. Let the AI work at it: it debugged step by step for a long time and pinpointed the exact error.

Ties back to the lessons: small sub-tasks, guide the AI, and use tests plus a gate as the review.
7:
Quick look under the hood. The first job of any engine is move generation: list every legal move.

The board is doing exactly that now: from the start position it makes and unmakes each of White's 20 moves. That's depth 1.

Click Depth 2: for each of White's 20 moves, Black has 20 replies. 400 positions.

Click Depth 3: 8,902 positions. Point at the table: depth 6 is already 119 million. It grows roughly 30 times per move. Engines generate millions of positions per second, and it still isn't enough to look at everything.

That's why move generation has to be fast and exactly right. One wrong move in here and the whole search is wrong. If you build one, this is where unit tests save you, and where you can lean on the AI's step-by-step debugging.
8:
Since you can't look at everything, the engine has to be smart about what it looks at.

• Search ahead: pick the move best for you, and assume your opponent picks the move best for them. That's minimax.
• Prune: skip lines that can't change the answer. That's alpha-beta.
• Evaluate the position at the end of each line: material, piece placement, king safety.

Walk the tree: on the left, the opponent's best reply leaves me at 3. On the right, the first reply already gives me only 2. Since 2 is worse than the 3 I already have, I don't need to look at the other replies. That's the pruning, and it's why engines can search so deep.

Note: this kind of 'AI' is search plus a scoring function, not a language model. The language model helps you write it.

Simple to describe, very hard to make fast and correct. That's where the AI helps, and where a gate like the 400 games matters.
9:
Alpha-beta is just the start. You need many more pruning techniques to make the search strong. Three examples:

• Null move pruning: let the opponent move twice in a row. If you're still clearly winning even after giving away a free move, the position is so good you don't need to search it fully.
• Late move reductions: sort moves so the most promising come first. Search moves late in the list less deeply. If one surprises you, search it again at full depth.
• Futility pruning: close to the end of the search, if you're far behind and a quiet move can't possibly make up the difference, skip it.

Each one is a trade-off: search less, risk missing something. Only a gate like the 400 games tells you if it's worth it.

The evaluation is just as important. A deep search with a bad evaluation still picks bad moves. In the past evaluation was hand-written: material, piece placement, king safety, with weights tuned by hand.

Today, use a trained neural network, called NNUE. It's trained on millions of positions and designed to update quickly as moves are made, so it's fast enough to run inside the search. That was one of the biggest jumps in engine strength in recent years.
10:
A tip if your project is performance-sensitive: in a chess engine, performance is everything. The faster the search, the deeper it sees in the same time, and the stronger it plays.

So ask the AI to set up benchmarking: small programs that run move generation, search and the neural network on fixed positions and measure the speed. On top of that, a profiler. On the Mac it's the built-in 'sample' tool, which checks a thousand times a second which function the program is in. On Linux, Valgrind's Callgrind. Make it all one command, for example: make profile.

Then the nice part: let the AI read the profiler output itself. It's a long text report of call stacks and sample counts. Tedious for you, easy for the AI. It quickly points out the hot spots, fixes them, re-runs the benchmark and confirms the speed-up.

Save the workflow as a skill, so the AI knows how to profile the project next time.

Takeaway: give the AI a way to measure. With hard numbers it can find and fix problems on its own, and prove the fix worked.
11:
One thing to stress: aim for improvement you can measure, not a feeling.

A lot of talk about AI productivity is gut feeling: 'it feels faster', 'the code seems better'. That's hard to prove.

If your domain allows it, find a hard metric. In chess, Elo comes from games played. Every change to ZeroG had to pass the gate: 400 games against the previous version, with a significant improvement. If it didn't, it was rejected, no matter how good the code looked.

And use an independent judge where you can. CCRL rates engines independently, by playing them against other engines.

Then the comparison is fair: years of my own work by hand gave 1863 Elo. One summer with AI gave 2666. That's over 800 Elo, and it's an objective number.

Takeaway: when you can benchmark, do it. It turns 'AI helped' into something you can prove.
12:
Next example: Jetpack. A good way to start is a simple game you like to play yourself. Mine is a retro 2D platformer where you fly a jetpack, collect emeralds and phase through walls.

I used Antigravity with Gemini 3.8, which had just been released. It was a big improvement over 3.6 Flash, both in performance and in speed. Development took less than a month.

You don't have to get the language right from the start. Gemini chose JavaScript. Later I asked it to convert the whole thing to TypeScript, which it did without much trouble.

Expect the feel of the game to be the hardest part for the AI. For me it was the turns: how the jetpack moves when you change direction in the air. It took several prompts and a lot of play testing before it felt natural and easy to steer.

You can generate all graphics and sound from prompts. Gemini made them in retro style.

The music too: prompt Gemini to take old classical melodies and play them in retro game style. Grieg's Hall of the Mountain King, Brahms' Hungarian Dance No. 5, Vivaldi, Mozart, Bach's Toccata and Fugue. (Click the screenshots: the music playing is from stage 6.)

And share it. I deployed it and played it online with friends and family, including multiplayer. It's free for everyone to play and has been played by about 60 players so far. The source is open on GitHub.
13:
Some lessons you can take from Jetpack.

When the AI struggles with a bug for a while, code quality easily gets worse. It tries one fix after another, and the leftovers stay in the code. So once the bug is fixed, prompt the AI to clean up the code.

For the AI to work well, keep the code in good shape: a good architecture, types and variables properly named, files and functions that aren't too large, not much duplicated code, and so on. Exactly as it is for us humans.

Use AI for refactoring. It's fast, it makes good changes, and things don't break. It almost seems to enjoy it.

Set up code coverage, and let the AI do it. I asked Gemini, and it did all of it itself. It chose c8, which uses the coverage that's built into Node's V8 engine, so the TypeScript code needs no instrumentation. It wrapped the whole test suite (about 40 test scripts run with tsx) in one command, npm run test:coverage, and configured it to report on the game client and the server, as plain text, an HTML report and an lcov file.

Then use it as input. The text report is a table of every file and which lines are never run. Perfect for the AI: let it read the report, pick the gaps and write new unit tests for them. The same day it added tests for the game, the multiplayer controller and the networking code.

The last report: about 62% of lines, 66% of branches and 75% of functions covered. Not 100%, but a lot for a hobby game, with little effort.

Same lesson as with the profiler: give the AI a way to measure, and it can find the gaps on its own.
14:
Now the main example: Terminal Depth.

A tip: test on a smaller project first. Jetpack was really just a first test, to see whether it was worth starting on my dream project: a modern version of a game I played a lot in the 90s. A 3D first-person shooter with six degrees of freedom, flying in tunnels and mines.

Don't be afraid of new ground. This was a much bigger step than Jetpack: 3D modelling and integrating with a real game engine. I looked at Unreal and Godot. And on top of that: online multiplayer combat.

(Click the video to play some gameplay.)
15:
Here's a pipeline you can use. Unlike with Jetpack, combine several specialised AI tools, each for its own job.

First, use ChatGPT to create concept images: enemies, the player's spaceship, weapons and other items in the game.

Then use that image to generate a 3D model with Meshy.ai, an AI tool made specifically for that purpose.

Copy the 3D models into the game's source code, and ask your coding AI to import them into the game. I used Gemini, and later Claude.

Now and then, use Blender for small manual adjustments to the AI-generated models, or to reduce the number of polygons for performance reasons.
16:
For music, try Google Gemini's online chat, which has a music plugin.

For sound effects, try ElevenLabs (elevenlabs.io).

For the engine I chose Godot, with C# for the game logic.

So the big difference from Jetpack: there, one AI did almost everything. Here, combine many specialised AI tools, and let the coding AI tie them together in the game.
17:
To give you an idea of what you can build: some facts about Terminal Depth.

The first commit was on 11 September, about two months ago.

On the left, the code: well over a hundred thousand lines. Most of it is C# game code, but there is almost as much test code as game code, plus a whole pipeline of Python and GDScript tooling for 3D models, textures, headless checks and rendering.

On the right, the content: close to a hundred scenes, dozens of sound effects, 3D models and textures, story voice lines, different enemy types, rooms and corridors, music, and several playable levels.

All in all, the downloadable game is over 500 MB.

In two months, as a hobby project.
18:
How do you keep a 115,000-line project on track with AI? With rules and skills.

Keep the project instructions in AGENTS.md, shared by every agent, so Gemini and Claude read the same rules. CLAUDE.md can just import it.

Put detailed rules in small files: audio, lighting, save/load, testing, coding standards and so on. I have 12. Let each rule say which file paths it applies to, so it is only loaded when the AI works in that area. That keeps the context small.

Skills are step-by-step procedures the AI finds by their description. Let the AI build them, for example the 3D model pipeline, model performance optimization, and level assembly.

Add a few hard rules of your own: never commit, so you review and commit yourself. Zero-warning build, every warning fails the build. And after every task, have the AI reflect on what was hard and propose improvements to the rules or skills, so you can approve with a simple yes. The rules grow with the project.

Tech debt: have the AI point it out, not fix it on its own. Otherwise every small task turns into a big refactor. Collect it and run dedicated cleanup passes, with saved prompts and written plans, for example a code quality plan for the UI code.
